about: How release versions rank, and what a contract ceiling entitles. The issuing side and the deployment both decide entitlement with this comparison, so a disagreement here is a disagreement about what was sold.

cases.name: compare 3.2 to 3.2.0
cases.why: a missing segment counts as zero, so these are one release

cases.name: compare 3.2.0.0 to 3.2
cases.why: trailing zero segments do not make a later release

cases.name: compare 3.10 to 3.2
cases.why: numeric segments rank as numbers, not as text

cases.name: compare 3.2 to 3.10
cases.why: the same comparison read the other way

cases.name: compare 3.2.0-rc1 to 3.2.0
cases.why: a segment that is not a number ranks lexically, above its base

cases.name: compare 3.2.0 to 3.2.1
cases.why: sharing a prefix does not make two versions equal

cases.name: compare  to 0
cases.why: a blank version is the lowest release there is

cases.name: compare  to 0.0.1
cases.why: and it ranks below anything above zero

cases.name: compare 10.0 to 9.9.9
cases.why: two digits do not rank below one

cases.name: compare 1234567890123456789 to 999
cases.why: a segment too long to read as a number ranks lexically

cases.name: 3.2.0 under ceiling Some("3.2")
cases.why: a release at the ceiling is entitled

cases.name: 3.2.1 under ceiling Some("3.2")
cases.why: a patch above the ceiling is not: the line was not sold

cases.name: 9.9.9 under ceiling Some("  ")
cases.why: a blank ceiling is no ceiling

cases.name: 3.1 under ceiling Some("3.2")
cases.why: anything below the ceiling is entitled

cases.name: sort key of 3.2
cases.why: short versions pad out to four segments

cases.name: sort key of 3.10
cases.why: padding is what makes a text sort rank 3.10 above 3.2

cases.name: sort key of 3.2.0-rc1
cases.why: a pre-release suffix stays beside its base
